tldr: This paper presents "DREAM," a framework that adapts real-world VLA models without human demonstrations. It automatically generates large amounts of training data in simulation using only a short smartphone video of the workspace and a natural language instruction.
hero_caption: The overall DREAM pipeline. It builds a digital twin from a real workspace video and natural language instruction using 3D Gaussian Splatting, defines symbolic goals with an LLM, plans motions via TAMP, augments trajectories, and renders photorealistic images to generate fine-tuning data for VLAs.
overview:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models are attracting major interest for general-purpose robot manipulation. However, deploying them to a new environment often requires workspace-specific fine-tuning data due to domain gaps in desk patterns, lighting, and camera poses. Collecting such demonstration data via human teleoperation for every workspace is a huge burden in both time and labor costs.

To address this, the authors propose "DREAM." The idea behind DREAM is simple and clear: take only a short video of the workspace and a verbal task instruction as input, construct a digital twin of the environment, and automatically generate robot motion trajectories in simulation. By decoupling appearance from physics—reproducing visual realism using 3D Gaussian Splatting while handling physics and motion planning with lightweight CAD and mesh models—it synthesizes executable, realistic data even for complex real-world scenes.

In experiments on a real xArm7 robot, the authors first confirmed that policy evaluation in the reconstructed simulator correlates strongly with real-world success rates ($r=0.98\sim 0.99$). Furthermore, scaling the automatically generated data to train VLAs (SmolVLA and $\pi_{0.5}$) achieved real-world task success rates that outperformed training on 100 human-collected teleoperation episodes.
contributions: Proposed "DREAM," a pipeline that automatically generates training data for real-world VLAs from only a short workspace video and natural language instructions, without any human demonstration collection.

Decoupled visual appearance (3D Gaussian Splatting) from physics and geometric planning (IsaacLab + TAMP), enabling the generation of executable, visually aligned data without high-precision mesh reconstruction.
Quantitatively demonstrated that policy evaluations in the reconstructed environment perfectly match the ranking of real-world performance (MMRV = 0.000).

Showed that although an automatically generated demonstration has lower sample efficiency than a human teleoperated one, scaling up using compute time can match or exceed human teleoperation performance on a real robot.

sections.heading: Can We Eliminate per-Workspace Data Collection Costs?
sections.summary: Pretrained VLA models tend to fail when deployed directly to new workspaces, making action-labeled adaptation data essential. Because human teleoperation for every environment is impractical, this paper introduces "DREAM," which autonomously synthesizes training data from a video and language instructions.
sections.details:
VLA (Vision-Language-Action) models are rapidly advancing as foundation models that directly output robot joint and end-effector actions from camera images and natural language instructions. However, when deployed zero-shot into new workspaces with unseen tables, lighting, object layouts, or obstacles that were not in their large-scale pretraining data, they still frequently fail.

Unlocking their full performance requires fine-tuning data tailored to the deployment workspace. However, having humans teleoperate robots to collect this data is painful. It ties up human operators for each workspace, requires safety monitoring, and forces people to manually reset objects in the real world whenever a failure occurs.

While recent studies have explored augmenting small amounts of demonstrations in simulation or reconstructing environments from scan data, almost all of them still require an initial "seed demonstration" collected by a human.

To tackle this, the authors developed "DREAM" (Deployment-Time Demonstration Generation via Real-to-Sim for Scalable Policy Adaptation). DREAM requires only a short video of the target workspace taken with an everyday camera, such as a smartphone, and a language instruction. It then fully autonomously generates workspace-specific training data without any human demonstrations. Through real-robot evaluations, the study investigates whether simulation can serve as a dependable training data source and how efficiently it scales compared to human teleoperation.

sections.heading: How Does DREAM Differ from Existing Data Generation Methods?
sections.summary: This section reviews related work, including planning-based demonstration generation, human demonstration augmentation, and real-to-sim reconstruction. DREAM is unique because it uses no seed demonstrations, plans long-horizon motions directly from language instructions using TAMP, and renders them in photorealistic reconstructed scenes.
sections.details:
Technologies related to this paper can be broadly categorized into three lines of research:

- Planning-Based Data Generation:
Methods that automatically synthesize robot trajectories using grasp planning or Task and Motion Planning (TAMP) instead of human teleoperation. Solving discrete task steps and continuous geometric trajectories together allows the generation of long-horizon task data. However, most previous methods operate in manually designed CAD simulation environments, leaving a significant visual sim-to-real gap compared to real camera images.

- Demonstration Augmentation from Human Teleoperation:
Approaches such as MimicGen that take just a handful of human demonstrations and transform or replay them across randomized object configurations in simulation to create thousands of trajectories. While highly efficient, these methods inherently rely on the availability of initial, high-quality human demonstrations.

- Real-to-Sim Reconstruction:
Research using NeRF or 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) to import real-world workspace appearances into simulators (e.g., RialTo, RoboSplat). While this drastically narrows the visual gap, existing works still copy object trajectories from human demonstrations or depend on reinforcement learning or simple scripted motions.

DREAM combines the best of these approaches. It replicates the workspace with high fidelity using 3DGS, while combining an LLM and TAMP to plan and augment multi-step executable trajectories entirely from scratch using only language instructions. Its key difference is that it completely removes the need for initial human demonstrations.

sections.heading: Inside DREAM: Decoupling Appearance from Physics
sections.summary: DREAM operates in four stages: digital twin reconstruction, TAMP demonstration synthesis, trajectory augmentation, and rendering into a dataset. Its core philosophy is decoupling visual realism (3DGS) from physics and motion planning (lightweight meshes) to generate executable actions without needing watertight meshes of complex real scenes.
sections.details:
The DREAM pipeline consists of the following four steps:

- III-A Digital Twin Reconstruction:
Camera poses are estimated from a handheld video using COLMAP, and the scene is optimized using 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS). Reconstructions from monocular video have ambiguous scale and coordinate frames. Instead of placing physical calibration markers, DREAM uses the appearance of the robot visible in the video. By creating a reference point cloud of the robot from its joint angles at capture time and combining SAM3 segmentation with multi-view voting, FPFH features, RANSAC, and scaled ICP, it automatically aligns the scene to the robot's base coordinate frame in meters. Furthermore, it decomposes the scene into background, robot links, and manipulable objects as distinct Gaussian assets. Object models are generated from a few photos using a 3D generative model (TRELLIS) and paired with collision meshes.

- III-B TAMP Demonstration Synthesis:
Symbolic task goals and success criteria needed for planning are generated by an LLM (GPT-4o-mini) by selecting and instantiating predefined predicates (e.g., On(x, y)). By preventing the LLM from inventing arbitrary semantics and enforcing grammar checks, the system avoids generating incorrect action labels caused by hallucinations. From the initial state, cuTAMP searches for PDDL skeletons, and a diffusion-based grasp generator (GraspGen), GPU-parallel particle optimization, and cuRobo joint-space trajectory planning generate collision-free, executable trajectories.

- III-C Demonstration Augmentation:
To reduce TAMP computational costs, DREAM takes a small set of source demonstrations (~50) and applies MimicGen-style trajectory transformations across randomized initial object configurations. Because the TAMP planning structure is preserved, subtask boundaries (such as post-lift poses) are accurately segmented, rigidly transformed to new object poses, and connected via interpolated motions. Invalid trajectories are filtered out using physical validity checks.

- III-D Rendering and Policy Learning:
Using the recorded joint and object trajectories, the decomposed 3DGS assets are recomposed to render camera views. Since all assets are merged into a single Gaussian set, occlusions between the robot and objects are naturally resolved via depth-sorted alpha blending without extra computation. The final output is formatted into LeRobot datasets to fine-tune VLA models.

sections.heading: Real-World Evaluation: Can Generated Data Outperform Human Teleoperation?
sections.summary: Validation was conducted on two tasks using an xArm7. Experiment 1 showed that simulator evaluation ranks policies identically to the real robot. Experiment 2 demonstrated that scaling generated data yields real-world success rates (up to 93.3%) that outperform models trained on 100 human demonstrations.
sections.details:
Real-robot experiments used an xArm7 robot and two RealSense cameras (a static over-the-shoulder camera and a wrist-mounted camera) across two tasks: the single-step "BlockIntoBowl" (placing a blue block into a red bowl) and the multi-step "FruitPacking" (sequentially placing a banana and a peach onto a red plate). Evaluated policies included the VLA models SmolVLA and $\pi_{0.5}$, along with Diffusion Policy as a baseline.

- IV-B Experiment 1: Sim-to-Real Correlation (RQ1):
To verify whether the reconstructed simulator serves as a reliable evaluation environment, identical policy checkpoints were evaluated in both simulation and the real world. Pearson's correlation coefficient was $r=0.98$ for BlockIntoBowl and $r=0.99$ for FruitPacking. The Mean Maximum Rank Violation (MMRV), which measures policy ranking reversals, was $0.000$ for both tasks, indicating perfect rank preservation. While success rates in simulation tend to be 7–14% lower than in the real world (pessimistic), the simulator ranks policy quality in the exact same order as the real environment.

- IV-C Experiment 2: Data Collection Time and Performance Scaling (RQ2):
VLA models were trained on human teleoperation data (10, 50, 100 episodes) and DREAM-generated data (100, 500, 1000 episodes) to compare real-world success rates.
When generated data was scaled to 1,000 episodes, $\pi_{0.5}$ reached a 93.3% success rate on BlockIntoBowl (beating 86.7% from 100 teleop demos), and SmolVLA reached 80.0% (beating 73.3% from 100 teleop demos). On FruitPacking, $\pi_{0.5}$ achieved 86.7%, surpassing the 80.0% achieved with 100 teleop demos.

In terms of cost, human teleoperation demands continuous human labor proportional to the number of demonstrations. In contrast, while DREAM requires fixed upfront compute time for video capture, alignment, and TAMP source demo generation (~36 minutes for BlockIntoBowl and ~95 minutes for FruitPacking), human active time is just a few minutes for video capture and instruction input. The wall-clock break-even points were 73 and 168 episodes, respectively; collecting data beyond these volumes makes DREAM faster even in total wall-clock time. Although generated data has lower sample efficiency per demonstration due to trajectory noise and redundancy, scaling up data collection using compute overcomes this drawback.

sections.heading: Conclusions and Future Outlook
sections.summary: DREAM is a promising framework for adapting VLA models using workspace videos and language instructions without extra human demonstrations. While currently limited to static environments and rigid bodies, extending it to deformable objects and contact-rich tasks represents key future work.
sections.details:
DREAM builds an executable digital twin from a short capture video and language task instructions, combining TAMP and trajectory augmentation to autonomously generate large amounts of fine-tuning data.

The framework demonstrates that the primary bottleneck of adapting VLA policies to new workspaces—collecting task-specific human demonstrations—can be significantly mitigated. In particular, the findings that simulator evaluation strongly correlates with real-world performance and that scaling synthetic demonstrations can match or exceed human teleoperation are notable milestones for practical robot foundation models.

On the other hand, the current system assumes static tabletop environments with rigid objects. As future directions, the authors plan to extend the framework to deformable objects (such as cloths and ropes), articulated objects, and tasks involving more delicate physical contacts.

takeaways: Decoupling visual realism (3DGS) from physics and planning (IsaacLab + TAMP) avoids the difficult problem of watertight real-world scene meshing while generating high-quality data.

Although automatically generated trajectories have more noise and lower per-sample learning efficiency than human demonstrations, scaling them by 10x using GPU compute allows them to surpass human teleoperation performance.
Simulators reconstructed and properly scaled from real environments preserve real-world policy rankings almost perfectly (MMRV=0.000), making them dependable offline evaluation benchmarks.
limitations: Currently restricted to static environments with rigid bodies resting on simple planar support surfaces, without support for deformable objects, articulated mechanisms, or complex contact-rich manipulation.
The time required by TAMP to synthesize initial source demonstrations (~50 episodes) increases sharply with task horizon, as lower planner success rates drive up fixed upfront compute costs.
Smaller capacity models with lower expressiveness (such as SmolVLA) struggle to tolerate noise in augmented trajectories on long-horizon tasks, leading to performance plateaus.
